articles.title: Norway's Princess Astrid dies two days after attending brother King Harald's funeral
articles.summary: Princess Astrid "represented the Royal House in a warm and dutiful manner", the new king, Haakon VIII, said in a tribute to his aunt.

blocks.text: Princess Astrid of Norway, the sister of the late King Harald V, has died at the age of 94, two days after attending his funeral, the country's royal palace has announced.
The new king, Haakon VIII, said that "throughout her long life, Princess Astrid represented the Royal House in a warm and dutiful manner".
Harald died last month, aged 89, after more than 35 years as king. His funeral was Astrid's last public engagement.
The princess will be buried at state expense and flags will be flown at half-mast across Norway, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.
Astrid was the last surviving child of King Olav V, who reigned from 1957 to 1991.
She became Norway's first lady at the age of 22 in 1954, after the death of her mother Crown Princess Märtha. Olav did not remarry and Astrid retained the title until her brother's marriage in 1968.
"In her work, Princess Astrid was always particularly concerned with care and inclusion for the most vulnerable in society," her nephew King Haakon said in his statement.
Her health had deteriorated in recent months and in March she received hospital treatment for pneumonia.
Dozens of European royals and heads of state attended Harald's funeral on Wednesday, including the Prince of Wales and three Nordic kings.
Thousands of people lined the route during a procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral on Wednesday afternoon.
The non-royal leaders paying their respects included Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier and five foreign prime ministers.

articles.title: US lettuce prices chopped as costs for other goods remain stubbornly high
articles.summary:
Price for the crop dropped dramatically this summer after the cyclospora outbreak caused demand to wilt

At the Republicans’ midterm convention held earlier this week, Donald Trump said that…

blocks.text: At the Republicans’ midterm convention held earlier this week, Donald Trump said that “food prices and almost every other item are rapidly going down”. Fresh inflation data on Friday told a different story – but in one specific case, costs have been chopped.
The price of lettuce dropped dramatically this summer after the cyclospora outbreak caused demand to wilt, with prices dropping even further in August, according to new data released on Friday.
The crop was closely linked to the diarrhea-causing parasite that has seen more than 19,500 confirmed cases in the US since May – 16 times the cases that were seen in the same period in 2025.

The outbreak spread to 20 states, with just more than 1,000 hospitalizations and two deaths, according to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The spread was linked to iceberg lettuce that has since been recalled, and the agency said that it “remains confident that all recalled iceberg lettuce related to this specific Cyclospora outbreak is off the market”.

There’s no dressing up the hit the lettuce industry has taken. New price data released on Friday showed that lettuce prices dropped another 6.2% from July to August. Prices had already gone down 16.4% the month prior, the largest decrease in recent history.

The economics behind food prices are often a mixed bag, but experts say there is a strong connection between lower lettuce prices and the cyclospora outbreak. As consumers learned about reports linking the parasite to iceberg lettuce, they stopped eating all types of greens.

“That’s a very consistent case here,” said David Ortega, a food economics and policy professor at Michigan State University. “People cut back on not just all lettuce, or a lot of lettuce, but even other produce just out of fear.”

This put many food chains in a crunch. Though Sweetgreen wasn’t linked to the outbreak, the salad chain cut its outlook for the year in August, citing a fall in foot traffic. Chipotle reported sales were down 2% in the second half of July, though the chain “maintains a very robust food safety program”. Taco Bell, which was directly linked to the outbreak, said it experienced a “meaningful” short-term impact on sales, though that had been “steadily improving”.

Before the outbreak, lettuce prices were increasing due to other supply constraints, including adverse weather and disease that were affecting harvests, Ortega said. The drop in demand seems to have somewhat stabilized lettuce prices to where they were a year ago: from August 2025 to August 2026, prices dropped just 2.2%.

It’s a tossup as to whether the drop in lettuce prices will alleviate any of the pain Americans have been feeling over higher prices. The ongoing war in Iran has boosted energy prices, with the US cost of diesel, which is essential for transportation within the supply chain, breaching $6 a gallon for the first time ever. Gas prices on average are $1.10 a gallon more expensive than last year, and fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, was up 52% for the year in August.
Trump’s trade war with Canada, one of the US’s closest trading partners, is also expected to affect prices, with tariffs expected to affect everything from liquor to toilet paper.

Canada is also a major agricultural trading partner with the US. Imports from Canada made up a total of 18.5% of the US’s total agricultural imports in 2025, according to the US Department of Agriculture. The US is Canada’s largest agricultural trading partner, buying up 60.3% of the country’s total agricultural exports.

Over the last few days, Trump – who last month said that “prices are coming down very rapidly” – has started to acknowledge that the economy for US consumers isn’t as rosy as he has portrayed. He voiced his prediction that oil prices will go “tumbling downward” after the election, as Iran is “desperate to try and affect the election”.

At the Republican convention, Trump said that he would give Americans a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans keep control of Congress after the midterms, a move critics said was a blatant bribe, and blamed Democrats for the higher prices.“I’m asking you to let us finish the job we began,” he said.

articles.title: Legarda camp slams ‘political persecution’
articles.summary: Environmental and constitutional lawyer Tony La Viña has described the plunder investigation involving Sen. Loren Legarda and her son, Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, as “classic…

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Environmental and constitutional lawyer Tony La Viña has described the plunder investigation involving Sen. Loren Legarda and her son, Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste, as “classic lawfare” and “political persecution.”
La Viña, who has stepped in as Legarda’s new spokesman, said the case was retaliation for Leviste’s public campaign against government corruption in late 2025.

He also defended Legarda against allegations involving Leviste’s Solar Para sa Bayan Corp. (SPBC), stressing that the senator has no corporate ties to the company, did not receive government funds and did not vote for the passage of its non-exclusive franchise.
“The senator does not own, run or take part in SPBC or any Solar Philippines company,” La Viña said.
“Being a parent and being a senator does not in any way prove she benefited, acted improperly or committed a crime,” he added.
La Viña also warned that the ombudsman’s approach to investigating unfulfilled renewable energy service contracts could discourage investment in the renewable energy sector.
Loren, son file counter-affidavits

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla yesterday confirmed that Legarda and Leviste had filed their counter-affidavits in response to plunder complaints involving alleged irregularities in solar energy projects amounting to P10.44 billion.

“They have already filed their counter-affidavits. They filed them late, if I’m right, but we’re not going to get them on any technicality. We will still consider the counter-affidavits,” Remulla said at a press briefing.
However, Remulla said the continued absence of the mother and son remains a stumbling block in the preliminary investigation as prosecutors may need to ask them questions.
Legarda has been on medical leave since Aug. 3 and extended her leave until the first week of September.
The ombudsman earlier flagged her extended medical leave, saying it raised suspicion.
The mother and son left the country on separate flights, with Legarda traveling to France and Leviste flying to Hong Kong.
Remulla said Legarda and Leviste were believed to be in Paris but had also traveled to Switzerland. The prosecution panel has 60 days to complete the preliminary investigation.
On One News’ “Stotrycon” yesterday, La Viña could not say where the two are or whether they would return, or what Legarda’s health problem is.

Investigators were considering legal measures to have them return to the Philippines, including the possible cancellation of their passports, to “preserve the integrity” of the proceedings before the anti-graft body and, if necessary, in court.

“If there is a prolonged absence and we can consider them fugitives from justice, then that is the time that we will move for the cancellation of their passports,” Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano earlier said.
Legarda has denied the allegations involving the solar power projects, calling them “false and baseless” and maintaining that no government money was involved.

articles.title: DILG seeks return of SK age limit to 15 –19
articles.summary: Youth officials should remain closely connected to the sector they are representing, said Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla as he is pushing for restoring the age of eligibility for the Sangguaniang…

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 12:00am

Department of the Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla at the budget deliberations in the Senate on Thursday (September 11, 2026). He recommended restoring the return of age eligibility for the Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) to 15 to 19 years old, saying youth officials should remain representative of the sector.
PNA photo by Avito Dalan

MANILA, Philippines — Youth officials should remain closely connected to the sector they are representing, said Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla as he is pushing for restoring the age of eligibility for the Sangguaniang Kabataan (SK) to 15 to 19 years old.

During the Senate committee on finance deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of the Interior and Local Government on Thursday, Remulla said the current age range allows people who may already be working or already starting to raise families to continue serving in councils intended for younger Filipinos.
“My recommendation is to bring it back to 15 to 19 years old, so that they would still be staying in the community,” Remulla said.
Under Republic Act 10742, or the Sangguniang Kabataan Reform Act, an SK official must be at least 18 years old but not more than 24 years old on the day of the elections.
“Because at 28 or 29, they may start settling down, having a family or working. I don’t think they are representative anymore of their constituents,” Remulla said.
Remulla pointed out that there is an overlap between the current SK age eligibility and the minimum age for other elective local posts, such as governor where the minimum age is 23.
The department chief likewise urged lawmakers to review the fiscal autonomy of SK officials, citing concerns over their capabilities to independently manage public funds.
Remulla cited the case of two SK chairpersons in Makati who were suspended for allegedly demanding a 20-percent kickback from a supplier and submitting documents with forged signatures.
“I think that the fiscal responsibility of the SK is not fully formed yet and they are subject to the manipulation of so many factors,” he said.

articles.title: Senate approves Philippines-France visiting forces pact
articles.summary: The Senate committee on foreign relations has approved the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOVFA) between the Philippines and France, paving the way for the treaty’s plenary ratification…

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 12:00am
Senate of the Philippines.
Graphics by Philstar.com / Enrico Alonzo

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate committee on foreign relations has approved the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement (SOVFA) between the Philippines and France, paving the way for the treaty’s plenary ratification next week.

Senate Majority Leader Juan Miguel Zubiri, who chairs the panel, said the pact would establish the legal framework for joint military exercises, disaster response operations and bilateral cooperation.
It also explicitly defines criminal jurisdiction over participating troops who commit offenses while in the country.

Once ratified, France will be the first European nation to have a SOVFA with the Philippines. It will also become the country’s sixth active visiting forces pact, joining agreements with the United States, Australia, Japan, Canada and New Zealand.

Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. backed the agreement during the hearing, citing France’s role as a major global arms supplier and its support for the 2016 Arbitral Ruling and freedom of navigation in the Indo-Pacific.
Teodoro also revealed that the Philippines is in its second round of SOVFA negotiations with the United Kingdom, while talks with other Asian countries are ongoing.

articles.title: President Marcos to represent Asean at BRICS Summit in India
articles.summary: President Marcos departed for New Delhi, India on Friday to attend the 18th BRICS Summit, where he is set to represent the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and push for peaceful settlement of…

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos departed for New Delhi, India on Friday to attend the 18th BRICS Summit, where he is set to represent the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and push for peaceful settlement of disputes under international law.
Marcos said his participation in the two-day summit comes at a critical time for the global economy, which he described as undergoing “profound changes” and pressure.

“We will engage the BRICS community, whose ranks include four of our fellow ASEAN member-states, on advancing our quest for peace, inclusive growth, regional resilience, sustainable development, food and energy security and a rules-based international order,” the President said in his recorded departure message.

“We have been asked to participate in the BRICS Summit at a time when the global economy is undergoing profound changes, even pressure. It is our conviction, however, that as a broader community of nations, it is imperative that we coalesce and cohere around issues that impact on us collectively,” he added.

BRICS, originally established by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, has since expanded to include other major emerging economies. The group serves as a platform for cooperation on economic, political and development issues.

The summit opens today, under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,” with discussions expected to focus on global economic uncertainties, digital public infrastructure, innovation and collective climate action.

“I will offer views on how partners can and should work in concert, if not together, to address these challenges, especially those that impact developing countries and emerging economies,” Marcos said.

“We will call for fairer global governance, stronger disaster preparedness, the responsible use of new technologies, climate action and the peaceful settlement of disputes under international law,” he added.
Meetings

On the sidelines of the summit, Marcos will meet Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi to review the implementation of the Five-Year Plan of Action for 2025-2029 under the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership.

“Our discussions will cover defense and maritime cooperation, trade and investment, the proposed Preferential Trade Agreement, health and pharmaceuticals, digital cooperation, tourism, direct air connectivity and people-to-people ties,” Marcos said.
He said the meeting would also be an opportunity to renew Manila’s invitation for Modi to visit the Philippines for the ASEAN-India Summit and the East Asia Summit in November.
Marcos is also scheduled to meet Indian business leaders as the Philippines seeks to attract investments in key sectors.

“Business and the economy are also important pillars of our ties with India. While in New Delhi, I likewise look forward to engaging Indian companies and players on why the Philippines should be part of their growth story,” he said.
“They will have plenty of opportunities to consider in infrastructure, digitalization, IT, pharmaceuticals, transport and logistics and other sectors critical to our development,” he added.
Indian companies pledged $5.8 billion in investments covering technology, health, energy and infrastructure during Marcos’ visit to India in August 2025.

articles.title: DFA to China: Move out, stop island-building in West Philippine Sea
articles.summary: The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) called on China yesterday to stop its occupation and island-building activities in Panganiban (Mischief) and Zamora (Subi) Reefs in the West Philippine Sea…

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) called on China yesterday to stop its occupation and island-building activities in Panganiban (Mischief) and Zamora (Subi) Reefs in the West Philippine Sea (WPS).

Asserting Philippine sovereign rights over the low-tide elevations, the DFA said both features fall within the Philippine exclusive economic zone (EEZ) and the country’s continental shelf in accordance with the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and as upheld by the 2016 Arbitral Award.
“We call on China to cease its illegal occupation and activities in Panganiban Reef and Zamora Reef immediately, and to abide by the final and binding 2016 Arbitral Award,” the DFA said.

The DFA noted that with low-tide elevations, “the Philippines exercises sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the features, and these can neither be the subject of a sovereignty claim nor capable of appropriation under international law.”

“China’s island-building on both features violates the Philippine Maritime Zones Act (Republic Act 12064) and UNCLOS, as confirmed by the Award, and does not change the features’ legal status as a low-tide elevation,” the DFA stressed.

“The department will continue to assert the Philippines’ sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the West Philippine Sea, and champion the Philippines’ legitimate rights and interests in the maritime domain,” the DFA said.

The DFA’s statement came after the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) fired multiple flares against an unarmed Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) aircraft conducting a maritime domain awareness flight on Monday.
Chinese forces occupying Panganiban and Zamora Reefs also issued radio challenges to the Philippine aircraft before landing on Pag-asa Island.

Meanwhile, Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. said that he sees more of the same assertiveness from China and expressed the need for partners to “change the way we react” during the 2nd Manila Strategy Forum organized by the Center for Strategic and International Studies on Thursday.

Speaking with Gregory Poling, senior fellow and director, Southeast Asia Program and Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative at the CSIS, Teodoro called out China’s increasing activities in the WPS, including the harassment of coast guard and naval vessels and aircraft, and their recent announcement of establishing a marine observatory in Panatag (Scarborough) Shoal or Bajo De Masinloc.

“As I keep on repeating, we are in a struggle; this is not going to be solved overnight. But I know that it’s not going to be resolved if we are not resilient, if we are not firm on our positions in not only the West Philippine Sea but the whole of the maritime domain of the Philippines to include our extended continental shelf,” Teodoro said.
In other regions, he noted that several European countries have not been shy about cyber and maritime threats like submarine cables, of which “they feel that China is threatening them.”

“So I think we see this assertiveness by China perhaps due to what they call ‘Xi Jinping Thought’ and the resurgence of a new China coupled with the Global South and a new international order, which is Sinocentric,” he explained.
“I think we will see more of the same. We should not expect any change in their behavior; what we should change is the way we react,” Teodoro said.
Research ship’s findings
The PCG is urging China to disclose the results and data gathered by its research vessel after spending 30 days within the country’s exclusive economic zone.
PCG spokesman for the West Philippine Sea Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela said the Chinese survey vessel Haiyang Dizhi Shihao left Philippine waters as of Friday morning.

PCG noted that the research ship entered the Philippine EEZ on Aug. 10 before arriving in Bajo de Masinloc (Panatag) a day later. It exited the shoal on Sept. 8 before leaving the country’s EEZ the following day.
“That is 30 days inside our EEZ, 28 of them off Bajo de Masinloc, without any permit from the Philippine government, as confirmed by the Department of Foreign Affairs,” said Tarriela.
The PCG said the research ship left Panatag Shoal a day after its activities were publicly reported and confirmed as unauthorized by the DFA.

“Chinese survey and research vessels rely on quiet, uncontested presence. Public disclosure denies them exactly that,” Tarriela said. “Transparency raises the cost of unauthorized marine scientific research in our waters and the evidence keeps showing that it works.”

Tarriela demanded that China publish the data it took while loitering in Philippine waters for over 30 days. “Whether Beijing responds or not, the Philippines puts on record that this activity was illegal and that information gathered in our EEZ belongs to the Filipino people,” he said. — Andrew Ronquillo

articles.title: NBI: Cayetanos expected back this weekend
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation sees no legal problem with the recent trip of Senators Alan Peter and Pia Cayetano to Singapore, with authorities expecting the siblings to return to the country…

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 12:00am
Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano speaks at a press conference at the Senate building on Monday, June 8, maintaining that he remains Senate president.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation sees no legal problem with the recent trip of Senators Alan Peter and Pia Cayetano to Singapore, with authorities expecting the siblings to return to the country this weekend.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag confirmed yesterday that his office is monitoring the lawmakers’ travel, acknowledging that while the trip is perfectly legal, its timing has naturally drawn public scrutiny.

“I think they’re going to Singapore for a vacation. That is their statement. And I have information that they will be coming back tomorrow probably, tomorrow (Saturday) 11 p.m. or Sunday 11 p.m. That was the information that reached me,” Matibag told reporters.

The public scrutiny stems from the NBI’s recent announcement that it will file cases in the coming days over alleged irregularities related to the “golden cauldron” installed for the 2019 Southeast Asian Games.
Matibag revealed that the bureau was ready to file a case but had to pause the process after critical witnesses surfaced earlier this week bearing new evidence.
The NBI is specifically scrutinizing the legality of Cayetano’s leadership over the Philippine Southeast Asian Games Organizing Committee (PHISGOC).
“He’s not a member of the board of directors of PHISGOC yet he always introduced himself as the chairman of PHISGOC, so that’s the line we are examining,” Matibag said.

Critics also pointed out the trip’s timing with the Department of Justice (DOJ)’s investigations into the obstruction of justice complaint against Sen. Alan Cayetano and Sen. Robin Padilla for allegedly helping fugitive Sen. Ronald dela Rosa evade arrest.
Matibag noted that the DOJ probe into the obstruction charges is practically concluded and is poised for resolution before being elevated to the ombudsman.
“There might be a resolution already as we speak and eventually, (the case) will move,” he added.

articles.title: Chances of nabbing Bato getting bigger – Jonvic
articles.summary: The chances of arresting Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa are getting bigger, according to Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, stressing law enforcement authorities would soon smoke the…

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 12:00am
Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The chances of arresting Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa are getting bigger, according to Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, stressing law enforcement authorities would soon smoke the fugitive senator out of his hideout.
Sought for an update on manhunt operations on Thursday afternoon, he told reporters talks are underway with Dela Rosa’s coddlers, refusing to discuss further details.
“The negotiations are ongoing and we will smoke him out sooner or later,” he said.
The interior secretary also clarified what he meant when he previously said the operations to arrest the senator could result in “body bags.”
“Body bags means if we go on full operations, a lot of people will die. That’s what it means,” he said.
Remulla said disclosing more information about efforts to arrest Dela Rosa could put people’s lives at risk but expressed confidence they will get the lawmaker from his lair.
Dela Rosa is facing an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court as a co-perpetrator in the crimes against humanity case of former president Rodrigo Duterte.
Remulla earlier this week said “very powerful people” are protecting Dela Rosa.
The senator was last seen in May leaving the Senate building shortly after a shooting incident. — Marc Jayson Cayabyab

articles.title: 2027 holidays: EDSA anniversary still a special working day
articles.summary: Malacañang released on Friday a list of regular holidays and special non-working days for 2027.

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 12:00am

A pedestrian passes the local EDSA People Power Monument along Congressional Avenue in Dasmariñas, Cavite on February 22, 2026 ahead of the 40th anniversary of the EDSA People Power revolution on February 25, 2026.
Ryan Baldemor / The Philippine STAR
MANILA, Philippines — Malacañang released on Friday a list of regular holidays and special non-working days for 2027.

Under Proclamation 1427, the regular holidays are New Year’s Day on Jan. 1; Maundy Thursday on March 25; Good Friday on March 26; Araw ng Kagitingan on April 9; Labor Day on May 1; Independence Day on June 12; National Heroes Day on Aug. 30; Bonifacio Day on Nov. 30; Christmas Day on Dec. 25 and Rizal Day on Dec. 30.?
Special non-working days are Ninoy Aquino Day on Aug. 21, All Saints’ Day on Nov. 1, Feast of the Immaculate Conception on Dec. 8 and the last day of the year on Dec. 31?
The EDSA people power revolution anniversary on Feb. 25 will be observed as a special working day.?
The special non-working days are Chinese New Year on Feb. 6; Black Saturday on March 27; All Souls’ Day on Nov. 2 and Christmas Eve on Dec. 24.?
The dates for Eid’l Fitr and Eid’l Adha will be declared in accordance with the Islamic calendar or upon Islamic astronomical calculations.
Meanwhile, Marcos declared Sept. 12 as a Day of National Mourning over the passing of National Artist for Literature Resil Mojares.

Mojares was cited for his contributions as a “teacher, scholar, essayist, fictionist and historian, which contributed in the promotion of regional literature and history, as well as the formation of Cebuano and national identity.”

articles.title: Edith Regalado, STAR’s Davao scribe, writes 30
articles.summary: Longtime STAR reporter Maria Editha Requina Regalado passed away on Sept. 9 at the age of 63 after a long health battle.

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 12:00am
DAVAO CITY, Philippines — Longtime STAR reporter Maria Editha Requina Regalado passed away on Sept. 9 at the age of 63 after a long health battle.
As in everything she did throughout her life, she faced her health problems with strength and grace.
She is survived by her children, Frances Hera and Joseph Noah, and her grandchildren, Kassandra Andrea, Joshua David Juat and Maria.
She was many things to many people: a beloved mother, a doting grandmother, a caring friend, a trusted colleague, a mentor and a pillar of the media community in Davao City.
She was a regular reporter for The Philippine STAR from January 2000 to March 2023, after which she became a correspondent.

articles.title: VP Sara calls on President Marcos to resign
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte called on President Marcos to resign, branding him the “problem of the nation” as she accused his administration of corruption, abuse and political harassment…

blocks.text: September 12, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte called on President Marcos to resign, branding him the “problem of the nation” as she accused his administration of corruption, abuse and political harassment amid the cases filed against her and members of her family.

“I cannot bring myself to just stay silent while I see you swimming through floods. Because I see you struggling so hard for your families. Because I witnessed the abuse of Marcos with my very own eyes,” Duterte told her supporters.
“Remember to keep calling for the departure of our nation’s problem, whose name is Bongbong Marcos. Resign, get out of there. You are a liar, you are abusive, you are corrupt,” she added.
Duterte likened Marcos to his father, former president Ferdinand Marcos Sr., whom she accused of ruining the country.

“My countrymen, our fight does not end here. Calling for the resignation of an addict will continue until it penetrates his broken mind – that he is the problem of this nation. Just like his father, who ruined our country, that is also what the son is doing,” she said.
Palace: Rushing to take over?

Responding to Duterte, Malacanang official Claire Castro said: “She wants the President to step down? Why? Is the Vice President rushing to take over [the presidency]? Their plan is obvious. So to our countrymen, be mindful of who the true leader is.”
Duterte said the cases involving her family should not be treated as political drama and instead pointed to what she described as abuses under the Marcos administration.
She cited the arrest of her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, and her ongoing impeachment proceedings as part of what she called schemes against her family.
“Marcos is fooling us right to our faces. Do not forget the time when the law was being broken right in front of us. Do not forget the corruption that they insist on hiding to this day,” she said.
She urged her supporters to continue fighting the administration, accusing Marcos of being ungrateful to the people who elected him.
“He has no sense of gratitude to the people. He has no sense of gratitude to everyone who went to the polling precincts to put him in office. He has no shame,” Duterte said.

“That is how it really is with an addict. Their thinking no longer passes through reality. Let us continue to fight against the abusive, the addicts and the corrupt,” she added. “This is not just our fight; this is our fight for our children.”
Deferred
Duterte made the statement following her supposed arraignment yesterday at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court, which was deferred after her lawyers filed a motion challenging the proceedings.
Her counsel, Paul Lawrence Lim, confirmed that the defense had filed a motion with the court but declined to disclose its nature out of respect for the proceedings.
“They granted the deferral so the Vice President will not be arraigned yet,” Lim told reporters.
Lim said Duterte continued to abide by the law despite questioning the court’s jurisdiction over the case.
“The Vice President is abiding to the law despite questioning the jurisdiction of the court, she still came to show that she is abiding by the law,” he said.

The defense also filed a petition for certiorari and prohibition with a temporary restraining order before the Supreme Court questioning a Department of Justice resolution, alongside its filing before the trial court.
The DOJ said it would respect the trial court’s decision and allow the judicial process to take its course.
Duterte posted bail last week after the court issued a warrant for her arrest over the three grave threats charges.

The DOJ case stemmed from a November 2024 online press briefing in which Duterte said she had hired someone to kill Marcos, First Lady Liza Marcos and then-House speaker Martin Romualdez if she were killed.
Despite the charges, Duterte said she would continue to face the cases filed against her.

“We will take each case as they come and we will answer each complaint as they come in,” she said. “Since 2023, I feel threatened. I feel harassed. I do not feel safe but I have a job that I have to do and I have an obligation to all of the people.”
Duterte vs Remulla
The legal proceedings also prompted a fresh exchange between Duterte and Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla over her arrest and the handling of the case.
Remulla earlier claimed Duterte wanted to be detained at Camp Crame following the issuance of the arrest warrant, saying authorities had prevented what he described as an attempt to create drama.
“They wanted drama. They wanted her detained. We didn’t allow it. We wanted to go according to the rules of law and the rules of court,” Remulla said.
Rejecting the claim, Duterte said: “He’s the one who wants the drama. The real drama, if you will see, was the arrest of Martin Romualdez.”
Remulla maintained that he was only doing his job and advised Duterte to focus on the legal and political issues confronting her.

“I think she has bigger things to mind than me. I’m just doing my job stating the facts,” Remulla said. “She has an impeachment going on. Maybe her energies are better focused on real world problems.”
Complaints
Duterte has also vowed to pursue legal remedies after the Taguig prosecutor’s office dismissed the first of two perjury complaints she filed against her alleged former bagman, Ramil Madriaga.
Duterte’s counsel and spokesman, Paolo Panelo, said the Vice President would not be deterred by the dismissal and would pursue the second complaint “whatever the odds.”

“If a complaint of that strength can be discarded, then the message is simple: a man may brazenly lie under oath against the Vice President and this administration will protect the lie if it is politically useful,” Panelo said.

“It would seem that they could not afford to do otherwise because this would amount to confirmation from the government itself that one of the bases for the impeachment against the Vice President was perjured testimony,” he added.
The Taguig prosecutor’s office dismissed the complaint for “lack of prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction.”

Duterte filed the complaint in March after Madriaga accused her of bankrolling her 2022 vice presidential campaign with “dark money” from drug lords and now-banned Philippine offshore gaming operators.
Case vs Padilla
Meanwhile, the DOJ said it has yet to issue a resolution on the obstruction of justice complaint against Sen. Robin Padilla over the alleged escape of Sen. Ronald dela Rosa.

DOJ spokesman Polo Martinez said the case remains under preliminary investigation, contrary to an earlier statement by National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag that the investigation had been completed and a resolution could already be forthcoming.
“The obstruction of justice case involving Senator Padilla is still currently undergoing preliminary investigation,” Martinez said.

The complaint filed by the Philippine National Police-Criminal Investigation and Detection Group stemmed from allegations that Padilla and others helped Dela Rosa’s alleged escape following the issuance of an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court. — Daphne Galvez, Emmanuel Tupas, Bella Cariaso

articles.title: Ukraine: Russian strike on Kyiv gas station kills 2
articles.summary: With fighting on the front lines mostly stalled, Russia has been increasingly hitting petrol stations and other civilian targets. Ukraine has also been attacking Russia with drones, killing three…

image.caption: Russia has struck around 300 petrol stations in Ukraine in recent monthsImage: AFP

blocks.text: At least two people were killed in Kyiv after Russian jet-powered drones struck a petrol station on Friday.
A 12-year-old boy was among 12 people who were injured by the attack, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said one of the injured was a first responder who was "wounded in a double-tap strike."

blocks.caption: Russia has turned to using jet-powered drones in near-constant attacks on KyivImage: Efrem Lukatsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russia increasingly targeting petrol stations with new, faster drones
Friday's drone strikes come a day after what is thought to be the first Russian attack on a Kyiv gas station during the war.
Russia has struck around 300 petrol stations in Ukraine in recent months, most of which were in or near frontline areas.
The attacks on petrol stations come amid a spike in Russian assaults using new, faster and harder-to-intercept jet-powered drones to strike logistics centers, warehouses and commercial supply chains.
Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down
Ukraine condemns escalating Russian 'terror'
Zelenskyy said Russia was escalating these strikes on civilian energy infrastructure, calling them "increasingly terrorist in nature."
"Maximum attention must be focused on protecting the skies, finding solutions to protect people, and scaling up countermeasures against Russian drones," the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.
The CEO of Ukrainian oil giant Ukrnafta, which owns the gas station and one other that was also struck on Friday morning, condemned Russia for "yet another deliberate strike on civilian facilities."
"There is no military objective in such attacks. This is terror against the civilian population," Bogdan Kukura said.
Russia has not publicly commented on the latest attacks, but has consistently denied targeting civilians.
Ukraine, Russia striking logistics, energy targets

More than four and a half years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion and with the fighting on the front lines in eastern Ukraine mostly stalled, Russia and Ukraine have been increasingly hitting logistics, energy and other economic targets in a bid to dent the other's war effort.
Ukraine has also stepped up its own drone attacks inside Russia. Overnight, two people were killed in Russia's Tula region, while one person was killed in Kursk on Friday, officials said.
Tula's regional governor Dmitry Milyayev added that three people were injured in the attacks.
Ozon, Russia's second-largest e-commerce platform, said a Ukrainian drone had struck a logistics hub in the city of Saratov, starting a fire.

blocks.caption: Kyiv says its strikes against e-comms targets are aimed at disrupting Russia's supply linesImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: More than 20 warehouses belonging to Ozon and Wildberries, Russia's other leading online retailer, have been hit in Ukrainian attacks in recent weeks.
Kyiv says the strikes are justified as part of its campaign to undermine Russia's war effort, which has also seen Ukraine target Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure.

articles.title: AfD’s new state MPs include ex-Stasi officer, former porn actor, neopagans and neo-Nazis
articles.summary:
Far-right German party’s newly elected representatives face fresh scrutiny as it tries to form government in Saxony-Anhalt

•

blocks.text: The Alternative für Deutschland is facing scrutiny over the suitability of some of its prospective new MPs – including a former Stasi officer and a former pornography actor – just days after its historic win in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Presented by the AfD’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, for a photocall in the state capital of Magdeburg on Thursday, some of the members-elect were revealed to have a range of questionable backgrounds, including criminal records, Stasi pasts and connections to far-right networks.

blocks.caption: The AfD’s newly elected members of the Saxony-Anhalt parliament. Photograph: Karina Hessland/Reuters

blocks.text: German media has revealed that among the 39 parliamentarians who will represent constituencies across Saxony-Anhalt in the state parliament, is a man alleged to have participated in pornography films and falsified academic qualifications; a former officer for the East German secret police, the Stasi; and several members under criminal investigation for their involvement in neo-Nazi organisations.

Two MPs are facing investigations into allegations they sought to continue the activities of the banned rightwing extremist organisation Artgemeinschaft, a neopagan group that has embraced nationalist and antisemitic ideas. The younger of the two is also alleged to have violated the law in relation to weapons, according to the public prosecutor’s office. Both reject the allegations.

The erstwhile pornography actor was convicted for stealing bedding in bulk from a hotel. A court confirmed he had been a pornography actor after he contested a local newspaper’s claims. He was expelled from a university after being found to have falsified his school leaving certificate, Die Zeit reported. The MP says he was readmitted after a legal challenge.

An ex-Stasi officer, aged 78, who won a direct mandate in his constituency, has admitted to having worked for the ministry for state security in the communist GDR, focused on East German citizens who wanted to permanently emigrate.
His role as an MP-elect has been criticised by campaign groups on behalf of victims of the former East German dictatorship.

Also, an investigation by the broadcaster ZDF revealed that some AfD ministers-elect who were also members of the previous parliamentary group, had ties to rightwing extremist groups. This included some having been members of the subsequently outlawed Homeland-Loyal German Youth group, HDJ. At one stage one of them had led the organisation, while an adviser to the AfD’s parliamentary group wrote a biography described as an “homage to national socialism”.
Among the prospective MPs are a number with pro-Kremlin links, as well as some who visited members of the Maga movement in Washington.

Asked to respond to the questionable biographies, in particular of the two MPs under criminal investigation, Siegmund, a former fragrance salesman who was unanimously re-elected as the AfD’s parliamentary group leader on Thursday, referred to the men in jest as “the bad guys” and said “we will await the results of the investigations and then discuss them”.

blocks.caption: Ulrich Siegmund at the AfD election party after polls closed last Sunday. Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters

blocks.text: Siegmund himself triggered fierce criticism during the presentation of his new parliamentary group after linking the production of arms in Germany to the party’s planned deportation offensive.
after newsletter promotion

In response to a journalist’s question about the planned opening of an Israeli arms company in the state, Siegmund said: “We do not categorically condemn the production of arms, because we will of course need equivalent resources for the future remigration and deportation offensive. This is also in the interest of internal security, our own instability and national defence.”

The statement was seized on by the party’s opponents. Katja Pähle, the chair of the Social Democrats (SPD) parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt, said Siegmund had issued a “political threat” by suggesting the use of “violence as a political tool”.
“This reveals the ugly face of a political system whose language and ideas are once again reminiscent of totalitarian models,” she said.

Whether the AfD, which secured 44% of the seats, forms a state government, which would make it the first far-right party to gain power in Germany since the second world war, will depend on whether it can find other like-minded MPs who might defect, or a single party willing to support the AfD. So far, the mainstream parties have refused to enter a coalition with the AfD, which has just under half of the 83 seats in the state, three short of an absolute majority.

Protests against the AfD are planned in more than 20 cities across Germany this weekend in response to the party’s win last Sunday, and ahead of two crucial state elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in Mecklenburg Vorpommen, where the AfD are predicted to do well.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: Who are the impeachment court's amici curiae?
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court has invited four retired Supreme Court (SC) justices to provide their expert opinions on the vote threshold needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: The Senate impeachment court has invited four retired Supreme Court (SC) justices to provide their expert opinions on the vote threshold needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte.
According to a report from GMA News Feed, all four retired SC justices have confirmed that they will provide their opinions. They were invited as “amici curiae,” or “friends of the court.”
Impeachment court spokesperson Atty. Reginald Tongol said three of the retired justices will give their opinions in person on September 16, while one will submit a legal memorandum.
Who are they?
Ret. Chief Justice Artemio Panganiban
Panganiban earned his Bachelor of Laws degree from Far Eastern University in 1960 and placed sixth in the Bar Examinations that same year.
Before former President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo appointed him Chief Justice in 2005, he served as an Associate Justice of the SC from 1995 to 2005.
His term as Chief Justice lasted less than a year before he retired in 2006.
During his 11 years on the SC, Panganiban wrote 11 books, one for each year he served on the court.
Panganiban is currently a columnist for the Philippine Daily Inquirer.
Ret. Chief Justice Reynato Puno
Puno succeeded Panganiban as Chief Justice in 2006. He earned his Bachelor of Laws degree from the University of the Philippines in 1962.
In 1967, he obtained a Master of Comparative Laws degree from Southern Methodist University in Dallas, Texas.
He later earned a Master of Laws degree from the University of California and a Doctor of Juridical Science degree from the University of Illinois in 1969.
From 1974 to 1982, Puno served as Assistant Solicitor General. He was also an Associate Justice of the Court of Appeals from 1980 to 1984 and again from 1986 to 1993.
He became an Associate Justice of the SC in 1993.
During his term as Chief Justice from 2006 to 2010, Puno introduced the Writ of Amparo and Writ of Habeas Data, both legal remedies aimed at protecting basic human rights.
Ret. Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna
Azcuna earned his Bachelor of Laws degree from Ateneo de Manila University in 1962 and placed fourth in the Bar Examinations that year.
He first served in government in 1963 as assistant private secretary to Court of Appeals Presiding Justice Jose Bengzon.
He later became Bengzon’s private secretary when Bengzon was appointed an Associate Justice of the SC in 1964.
In 1971, Azcuna became a member of the Constitutional Convention as a representative of Zamboanga del Norte. He was also a member of the Constitutional Commission that drafted the 1987 Constitution.
Azcuna served as Presidential Legal Counsel, Press Secretary, and Presidential Spokesperson during the administration of the late President Corazon Aquino.
Former President Arroyo later appointed him as an SC Associate Justice in 2002.
After retiring from the SC in 2009, Azcuna served as chancellor of the Philippine Judicial Academy for 12 years, until 2021.
Ret. Chief Justice Hilario Davide Jr.
Davide earned his Bachelor of Laws degree from the University of the Philippines in 1959.
He was also a member of the 1971 Constitutional Convention, representing the fourth district of Cebu.
From 1978 to 1984, Davide served as an assemblyman of the Interim Batasang Pambansa.
He was a known oppositionist during the administration of the late President Ferdinand Marcos Sr. and became the first minority leader of the Interim Batasang Pambansa.
In 1986, he became a member of the Constitutional Commission and chaired its Committee on Legislative Power.
Davide was the principal author and sponsor of Article VI of the 1987 Constitution, which covers the legislative department.
He served as chairman of the Commission on Elections from 1988 to 1990.
From 1989 to 1991, he led the presidential fact-finding commission that investigated the coup attempts against then-President Corazon Aquino.
Davide was appointed an Associate Justice of the SC in 1991. Former President Joseph Estrada appointed him Chief Justice in 1998.

As prescribed by the Constitution, Davide served as the presiding officer of Estrada’s impeachment trial. He also administered the oath of office to Arroyo when she assumed the presidency during EDSA Dos.
Davide retired from the SC in 2005.
Tongol said Davide would be the one to submit a legal memorandum.
The oral arguments between the defense and prosecution panels, meanwhile, will be held a week later, on September 23. Each side will be given 15 minutes to present its position.
Senator-judges are also expected to cast their votes on the same day.
Presiding Officer Senator Francis Escudero reiterated that at least 16 votes, or two-thirds of all 24 senators, are needed to convict, in accordance with the Constitution. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: US commemorates 25 years since 9/11 terror attack
articles.summary: A quarter century has passed since Islamists hijacked four commercial jets and turned them into weapons against the US. On Friday, ceremonies in New York, Pennsylvania and Washington DC marked the…

image.caption: The attacks of September 11, 2001, killed nearly 3,000 people, changing New York, the US and the worldImage: Angelina Katsanis/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Commemorations are being held across the United States on Friday to mark the twenty-fifth anniversary of the deadliest attacks ever carried out on US soil.
Events are taking place at the sites of the attacks — in New York City, Washington DC and Shanksville, Pennsylvania — and elsewhere around the nation to honor the 2,977 people killed that day.

The main ceremony is being held in New York, where Islamists from the terror group al-Qaeda flew two hijacked commercial airliners into the twin towers of the city's famous World Trade Center — a symbol of American economic power.
New York Mayor Zoran Mamdani, Governor Kathy Hochul and former Presidents Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden are in attendance as well as current Vice President JD Vance.
Friday's event will feature wreath layings and vigils, punctuated by several moments of silence, marking the moments of impact and collapse and honoring the memory of the dead.
Family members will read out the names of the people killed that day, as well as six that were killed in a 1993 al-Qaeda bombing in the building's basement.
This year, the ceremony also acknowledged more than 600 firefighters who died from illness related to the toxic air and dust emanating from the burning structures of the site.
In Washington, President Donald Trump spoke at a ceremony at the Pentagon, the symbol of the US' military might, which was also targeted with a hijacked airliner that day.
In his remarks, Trump referenced his ongoing war in Iran, saying the US will never forget 9/11, adding, "that's why we fight today."

Other administration officials are headed to the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. It was there that passengers stormed the cockpit of a hijacked United Airlines jet in midflight, forcing the plane to crash in an empty field and keeping attackers from hitting their final target, the US Capitol.
25 years later: Keeping the memory of 9/11 alive
EU and NATO allies honor victims
European Union and NATO allies also commemorated the event.
European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday expressed admiration for "victims, their families and those who rushed to help others."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen underscored the strength of democracies, pointing out that the attackers had failed to rob democratic nations of their freedom.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte posted on X that allies had, "stood together" that day, "invoking Article 5 for the first and only time in NATO's history."
Rutte added, "America's friends and allies in NATO stood with you then and we stand with you today."
US President Trump has often threatened to attack NATO allies and voiced doubt about alliance members' commitments to helping the US in times of need.
How did the 9/11 terror attacks shape modern America?
The world after 9/11
The audacious attack quite literally changed the world, stunning the US and triggering a chain of events that impact people's everyday lives to this day.

The incident sparked the Bush administration's "War on Terror," which drew the US into its longest-ever military conflict in Afghanistan and shattered trust in the nation when Bush insisted on invading Iraq, which was not involved in 9/11.

America's reputation suffered as a result of extrajudicial policies such as renditioning and "enhanced interrogation" at secret CIA prisons, as well as its creation of a detention facility in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, where suspected terrorists were held for years in dystopian conditions without trial.
The aftereffects of the wars are still costing the US billions and the debacle of Iraq irreparably damaged the solidarity the US was shown in the immediate aftermath of 9/11.

The attacks changed airport security measures, as well as the US government's ability to surveil citizens — leading to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security, one of the biggest agencies in the US government, and passage of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) and the USA Patriot Act.
Further, the event dramatically changed attitudes towards Muslims.

There was much controversy this year over whether Mamdani, for instance, should attend the New York ceremony. Republicans argued against it but the mayor insisted he would do so out of love of city and country and respect for those who died that day and in the years after.
This year's ceremony honors those who have died in the aftermath of the attack

Mamdani's election as mayor shows just how far parts of the country have come since that day and the young Muslim Democrat this week opened a new chapter in the story of 9/11 by releasing tens of thousands of documents showing that leaders had hidden information about the toxicity of air in the city after the attack.
As asbestos and toxic smoke blanketed the city for months officials told residents and clean-up workers that they had nothing to fear.
In fact, the toxicity of dust, rubble and smoldering plastic and metal has led to at least 9,400 additional deaths according a federal medical monitoring program.
9/11 survivor recalls his escape from WTC

articles.title: Americans mark 25 years since September 11 attacks amid enduring grief, reflection
articles.summary: For many whom the attacks directly affected — the victims' families and friends, first responders and rescue workers — the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter…

blocks.text: IN MEMORY. Members of the families of Flight 93 victims gather at the crash site of the hijacked airliner to take part in a family ceremony on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, in Stonycreek Township near Shanksville, Somerset County, Pennsylvania, US, on September 11, 2026.
Nathan Howard/Reuters

For many whom the attacks directly affected — the victims' families and friends, first responders and rescue workers — the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter century ago and the heartbreak that followed

items: On the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks, Americans commemorated the nearly 3,000 victims with ceremonies at Ground Zero, the Pentagon, and Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
Family members of victims read the names of those lost, including a new moment of silence for those who have died from 9/11-related illnesses, highlighting the ongoing impact of the tragedy.
The attacks have shaped US foreign policy and public attitudes, leading to a generation that has grown up with the repercussions, including increased prejudice against Muslim Americans.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Twenty-five years after the deadliest attack on US soil, Americans paused on Friday, September 11, to commemorate the nearly 3,000 people killed when hijacked planes slammed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and a field in Pennsylvania — and to wrestle with the consequences of September 11 that reverberate to this day.

In New York, family members of the victims, many carrying pictures of their loved ones, joined Vice President JD Vance and four former US presidents at Ground Zero in lower Manhattan. The ceremony began, as always, at 8:46 am with a moment of silence to remember the shocking instant when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Center’s North Tower.

Shortly after, victims’ family members began reading aloud the names of all 2,977 people who died on September 11, as well as the six people killed in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, a somber recitation that will last for hours. In a reminder of the time that has passed, some readers were children who had never met the relatives they lost in 2001.

Other moments of silence, marking when the other three airplanes crashed and the two towers collapsed, will follow. For the first time, a seventh silence will be observed to honor the thousands who have died since 2001 from illnesses tied to the toxic dust that poisoned the air for months afterward.

Gregory Carafello came to the ceremony to honor the memory of his lifelong friend James Martello, who worked at Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial firm that lost more than 650 employees in the attacks. Carafello himself was on the 18th floor of the South Tower but managed to evacuate.
“Everyone should realize that it was a very bad, catastrophic day for many families,” he said. “These were not warriors. These were people like you and me going to work.”

In Arlington, Virginia, senior military leaders gathered amid heavy rain early on Friday to watch the unfurling of an American flag at the west side of the Pentagon where American Airlines Flight 77 hit, killing 184 people in all. President Donald Trump is expected to speak there later in the morning.

Mourners were also gathering in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, at the crash site where passengers brought down one of the four hijacked jetliners, United Airlines Flight 93, that had been headed for Washington.
The attacks shaped generations of Americans who lived through the day or grew up in its aftermath, influencing US foreign policy, domestic politics and public attitudes toward security.

But for many whom the attacks directly affected — the victims’ families and friends, first responders and rescue workers — the anniversary is a tribute to the lives lost on a clear blue day a quarter century ago and the heartbreak that followed.
Caroline Ogonowski’s father, John, was the captain of Flight 11, which took off from Boston 47 minutes before striking the North Tower.
Ogonowski, now 39, had her first baby this year and named him after her father. She brought him her father’s grave last week and attended a memorial ceremony in Boston on Friday.

“This year, there’s this new sadness in knowing that they won’t ever get to know each other,” Ogonowski, who has worked in disaster relief and humanitarian assistance, said in a phone interview. “My father will never know his grandson. And my son will never know his grandfather.

“We owe it to my father and all the others that we lost on that day to make sure that we continue to teach future generations about what happened, about who these people were, who these heroes were, how our country came together and became stronger because of it,” she added.
A generation of Americans has grown up since 2001 who are too young to remember the attacks but whose lives were fundamentally altered by them.

The attacks initiated the “war on terror,” which led to the US invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq that lasted years. The resulting public backlash helped fuel Trump’s rise a decade ago, when he vowed not to start new foreign entanglements — a promise being tested by the current Iran war.
At home, Americans expressed deep solidarity and patriotism, as well as sorrow, in the immediate wake of the attacks.

At the same time, however, Muslim Americans and immigrants from Muslim-majority countries faced a rise in prejudice and hate crimes. Public polls have found 9/11 colors Americans’ perceptions of Muslims to this day. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, has faced calls from some Republicans to skip Friday’s ceremony, which he rejected.

Casualties were not limited to those who perished on September 11. Many rescue workers who spent weeks or months at the site afterward, as well as nearby residents and others, were sickened by toxins in the air and eventually died.

The New York City Fire Department lost 343 members on September 11. More than 600 additional firefighters, including some retired members who took part in the rescue effort, have died of 9/11-related illnesses since then, department figures show.
Twenty-six have died this year alone. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Palawan ferry fire death toll jumps to 35
articles.summary: As families wait for news of missing relatives, some express frustration at the lack of information they are receiving

blocks.text: AFTERMATH. A drone view shows emergency workers accessing the burnt MV June Aster ferry, a day after a fire broke out on the vessel, off the coast of Palawan, Philippines, on September 11, 2026.
Philippine Coast Guard/Handout via Reuters
As families wait for news of missing relatives, some express frustration at the lack of information they are receiving

items: Rescuers recovered 30 bodies from a burned ferry in Palawan, raising the death toll to 35, with 84 people still reported missing.
Survivors described the rapid spread of the fire, which trapped many passengers, while families expressed frustration over the lack of information about their loved ones.
The incident is part of a troubling pattern of maritime accidents in the Philippines, with the ferry carrying over 130 people and various vehicles when the fire broke out.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
PALAWAN, Philippines – Philippine rescuers recovered 30 bodies from a burned-out ferry on Friday, September 11, raising the death toll from the blaze to 35, authorities said.
Firefighters found the remains after they gained access to the vessel for the first time, having extinguished a fire that had hampered search and rescue efforts since Wednesday night, September 9.
Responders in protective suits were seen carrying black body bags from a small boat onto a Coast Guard vessel, video footage released by the Coast Guard showed.
Thick smoke and extreme heat had earlier prevented rescuers from entering the ferry, which was carrying more than 130 people when it was engulfed in flames.
As families waited for news of missing relatives, some expressed frustration at the lack of information they were receiving.

It was not immediately clear how many people remained unaccounted for, but authorities had reported 84 missing before Friday’s recovery of 30 bodies. The number of rescued stood at 43 as of Friday morning.

Images released by the Coast Guard showed the destruction caused by the fire inside the ferry, with rows of accommodation berths reduced to twisted metal and ash. One image showed what appeared to be skeletal remains amid charred debris in a heavily damaged section of the vessel.
Another photograph appeared to show a burned vehicle.

“We recognize the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident. Rest assured that operations are carried out with utmost respect for the deceased and their bereaved families,” Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemi Cayabyab said.

Richard Marceliano, one of the survivors, told GMA News he saw a small amount of smoke that quickly turned into a raging fire and spread through the ferry within seconds. He said he and other passengers spent nearly two hours floating in the sea before they were rescued.

The fire is the latest in a string of deadly maritime accidents in the Philippines, an archipelago of more than 7,600 islands where millions rely on ferries and small boats to travel between provinces and islands.
In January, more than 60 people died when a passenger vessel, carrying more than 300 people, sank en route to the southern province of Sulu.
As the search continued, stories of those still unaccounted for began to emerge.
A trip meant to celebrate a renewal of wedding vows instead brought grief and uncertainty for Jonnsban Tibay, 60, who fears his wife, Eden, was among those trapped on the ferry.

He had not accompanied her, and the couple was on a video call as the fire broke out. “She said, ‘We’re leaving now.’ I told her not to hang up and that we should keep the video call going. I was about to ask her to join our prayer when the call suddenly cut off,” he said.
Tibay does not believe his wife was able to escape.
“I’m 100% certain she didn’t jump. She must have been trapped,” he said. “She was diabetic and physically weak. She was no longer as agile as before.”
“It hurts so much,” Tibay said. “My two children can’t stop crying.”
At a port in Coron, Myra Bilan, whose sister and brother-in-law are missing, sobbed. Bilan, 47, said the couple had been traveling to Palawan on business to deliver beds.
“I hope our government takes action. So many people have died,” she said. “I hope they don’t turn a blind eye to poor families like us.”
Outside the office of shipowner Atienza Inter-Island Ferries in Manila, frustrated relatives waited for information about their loved ones.
The ferry company has said it was fully cooperating with government authorities investigating the incident.
It remained unclear what started the blaze, which broke out as the ferry neared the end of its more than 20-hour voyage to Coron, a popular tourist spot in northern Palawan.
A statement from the Maritime Industry Authority, citing survivor accounts, said two successive explosions were heard from within the ship, triggering the fire.
The ferry, with capacity for 330 people, was also carrying five motorcycles, an electric vehicle, a forklift, a pickup truck, and other cargo, according to the Coast Guard. – Rappler.com

articles.title: How 9/11 brought these 2 women together — over a piece of dried fish in Newfoundland

image.caption: Jeanette Gutierrez survived 9/11, while Kelly Sceviour helped stranded airline passengers in Gander, N.L. When the two women met years later, they formed a close bond. (Submitted by Kelly Sceviour)

blocks.text: The Current
Jeanette Gutierrez survived 9/11, while Kelly Sceviour helped stranded airline passengers in Gander, N.L. When the two women met years later, they formed a bond as close as sisters.
New Yorker and Newfoundlander met over a piece of dried fish in Gander
Jeanette Gutierrez grew up with one sister, but now has two.
Her sister, Gail, saved her life when Gutierrez was working across from the World Trade Center during the Sept. 11 attacks, 25 years ago.

But the New Yorker says she met her friend-turned-sister in Gander, N.L., a decade ago. She was attending a 9/11 commemoration in the small Canadian town, where dozens of flights were diverted in the hours after the attacks. With thousands stranded, Newfoundlanders stepped up to offer shelter.
Gutierrez wanted to meet the people behind that kindness, she told The Current.
“I decided to come here on a tour of gratitude to basically thank the people of Newfoundland for doing such a wonderful thing,” she said.
But once in Gander, she found herself staring down the stinky eye of a tiny fish, as she was being screeched-in.
“I don't eat seafood anyway. Not cooked and certainly not a stinky, little skinny fish. But I had to do it — I wanted so badly to be an honorary Newfoundlander,” she said.
Her salvation came in the form of a local woman, Kelly Sceviour, who spied her discomfort.
“She's a New Yorker so you could tell by her face what was happening … the look on her face was like, I am not [eating this!],” said Sceviour, the town’s special events co-ordinator.
Sceviour motioned to Gutierrez, indicating she should take a small bite and hand over the rest, which she promptly disposed of.
When the ceremony was over, Gutierrez approached Sceviour at the bar.
“[She] said, ‘I owe you a beer,’” Sceviour recalled. “And I was like, ‘Well, I don't drink beer, but I'll take a vodka!’”
“That's when we became friends.”

That friendship has blossomed into both women feeling as close as sisters, which Gutierrez says has helped her navigate the memories of 9/11. While she feels a kinship and comfort with other survivors, she says she finds it hard to be in New York on the anniversary, often travelling to Gander instead.
“I still get to honour and mourn and cry … everything that I do in New York. But I do it — for me — in a better place. In a place that I can also smile and laugh and be with this sister.”
My big sister saved my life
On the morning of the attacks, Gutierrez was working at Three World Financial Center, when she heard the first plane hit the North Tower at 8:46 a.m.

She called her sister Gail, who also worked downtown. Like many people, Gail initially thought there had been an accident. But when the second plane hit, Gail called back, urging Gutierrez to leave — she hesitated.
“Eventually she convinced me to leave by saying she would come to me and we would leave together,” Gutierrez said.
‘Thank God for them’: 9/11 travellers recount Canadian kindness
Gutierrez says if Gail hadn’t persuaded her to leave when she did, she might have been caught in the towers’ collapse.
“My big sister Gail saved my life that day.”
In Gander, Sceviour was working for the municipal government when she heard something had happened. She was sent home, but told she might be needed later.
Sceviour went to her mother’s house, which was right on the flight path for Gander International Airport.
“I watched as plane after plane descended. And I thought, 'Oh dear, what are we going to do with all these people?'”

Sceviour was called back into work at midnight, where she spent the night taking phone calls from people looking for loved ones on redirected flights. Working off a passenger list, she was able to reassure them that their family members were OK.
“To hear that relief in their voice … it felt really good to be able to help,” she said.
An unbreakable bond

Dozens of planes were redirected to airports in Newfoundland and Labrador that day. Gander took in nearly 7,000 stranded passengers, hosting them for several days as the community stepped up with food, accommodation and whatever assistance they could provide.
“We're born and raised in Newfoundland to be those kind and helpful and compassionate people,” she said.
Canada’s relationship with the U.S. has grown tense in recent years, as U.S. President Donald Trump launched a trade war and repeatedly threatened to use economic force to make Canada the 51st state.

items: Terror, tragedy, heartbreak and healing: How 4 Canadians are building a positive legacy 20 years after 9/11

blocks.text: But Gutierrez said politics can’t break her bond with Sceviour, and nothing can ever erase what the people of Newfoundland and Labrador did 25 years ago.
“Nobody sitting anywhere in any office can change who Canadians are,” Gutierrez said.
“It might change some relationships. It will never change ours.”
Audio produced by Alison Masemann.
